title: Ayyub's du'a
hook: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful (21:83)

segments.voice: Yesterday: faqir, in need, and Musa's open prayer in the shade. Your line was in need of any good. Today, a prayer from someone who'd lost far more.

Hospital waiting rooms have their own language. Some people go silent. Some rage. Some bargain: if you fix this, I'll do anything. Ayyub, Job, was struck by illness, and commentators say he lost his wealth and his family too. Stories people tell describe years of it, in vivid detail; the Qur'an gives no number and no gore. What it does give is the prayer he finally prays. A single verse, and it doesn't ask for anything.

Surah al-Anbiya, verse eighty-three, in Pickthall's translation: Ayyub cries to his Lord, "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic: anni massaniya d-durr, wa anta arhamu r-rahimin. Two statements, side by side. Harm has touched me. And You are the most merciful of the merciful. That's all. He doesn't say heal me, or why me. He doesn't list what he's lost. He tells the truth about his pain and the truth about Allah, and leaves the two next to each other. Scholars have long pointed to this as a model of courtesy in asking, adab: the need laid out, the mercy named, and the One who's merciful trusted to connect them. The verb is massa, to touch: harm has touched me, the Qur'an's ordinary word for affliction reaching someone, used without drama. The next verse gives the answer: We heard him, removed the harm, and restored his family to him, and the like of them with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship. Surah Sad adds the scene. He's told: strike the ground with your foot; here is cool water to wash in and to drink. And Allah describes him: We found him patient; how excellent a servant; he was always turning back. Patience, in Ayyub, isn't silence. It's saying the hard thing and the true thing in one breath, and not letting go of either.
screen: `ADAB: SAY THE NEED, NAME THE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Let someone who is ill come to mind, in body, in mind, or in grief, and picture them where they are right now, a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen, without rushing to fix it. If you pray, recite Ayyub's own words from 21:83 while you hold them in mind; if you don't, hold both truths: they're hurting, and they're not alone.
Ayyub's du'a. Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful: a prayer that names the pain and the mercy, and asks nothing more. Today's word.
Your line: you are the most merciful. The pain and the mercy, side by side. Day six hundred ninety-one, done.

howItsDone: Muslims who are ill, or praying for someone who is, often recite Ayyub's du'a (21:83); visiting the sick is a strongly encouraged practice in Islam.

what a scholar hears: scholars cite 21:83 as adab in du'a: state the need, name the attribute, ask nothing explicit; massa, to touch, is the Qur'an's usual verb for harm reaching someone (as in 2:214).

chat.says: What did Ayyub pray when he was sick? Did he ask to be healed?
options: He said harm has touched me, and You are most merciful, and left it there.
He demanded to know why this was happening after all his worship.
He promised to do anything at all, if only God would heal him.
chat.meaning: 21:83: adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy. He names the pain and the mercy, nothing more.

Ayyub.meaning: the prophet known in English as Job

adab.meaning: courtesy, good manners, here in asking

massa.meaning: to touch: the Qur'an's word for affliction reaching someone

arhamu r-rahimin.meaning: the most merciful of the merciful

notes: Pickthall wording of 21:83 quoted from memory; please confirm.
Popular accounts of Ayyub's illness (many years, graphic details) come largely from later narratives; the script says the Qur'an gives no number. Confirm framing.
The adab reading of 21:83 is a common scholarly observation; confirm.
'Lost his family' follows 21:84 (his household restored) and commentary; confirm.

Reviewer softened the hook: the Qur'an mentions harm and a restored household, so loss of wealth and family is now attributed to commentators rather than stated as settled. The screen line and fork setup still say health, wealth and family gone; confirm that's acceptable shorthand.
The practice adapts 21:83 for a third person (harm has touched them). It's Ayyub's words reshaped, not a new prayer, but a Keeper should confirm this use is fine.
